name: Cryolode
description: Cryolode gleams white and steel-blue under a distant sun, its ice shell fractured by ridges and pressure cracks that spider across entire hemispheres. Frozen methane lakes pool in the equatorial basins, their surfaces dark and unnervingly smooth. Where tidal flexing pulls the crust apart, geysers loft plumes of vapor that freeze into glittering arcs kilometers high.

The silence is absolute except for the groan of shifting ice, a sound felt in the chest more than heard. Surface temperatures would flash-freeze exposed flesh in seconds, yet drill cores hint at warmth far below, where a liquid ocean laps against a rocky core. In the ice caves near the south pole, trapped bubbles scatter light into curtains of blue aurora.

A fuel consortium tunneled into the crust to extract helium-3 trapped in the ice lattice, sinking a mining complex four kilometers down before the drills pierced the ocean ceiling and something flooded the lower galleries. The crew evacuated, leaving the station sealed and its distress beacon cycling on repeat ever since. Microbial life discovered in the ocean samples made the site a biological preserve by court order, though the ruling predates the beacon's strange new pattern.

The helium-3 reserves beneath the shell remain the largest known outside the gas giants, and platinum group metals stud the core-mantle boundary within reach of patient drillers. Corporations lobby to overturn the preserve status while preservationists guard the beacon transmissions as evidence of something living in the deep ocean. The next expedition to breach the ice will decide whether Cryolode becomes a fuel depot or a first contact site.
